name: Maine

notes: Groceries: grocery staples are exempt. Candy, soft drinks, bottled water and ice, snack foods (chips, crackers, granola bars, processed nuts), bakery desserts and ice cream, and sandwiches and salads are not grocery staples and are taxed at 5.5%, and food the seller prepares at 8%, which is not counted here.

Alcohol bought in stores: beer, wine and spirits bought in stores are taxed at 5.5% (drinks served in licensed establishments are taxed at 8%, counted for drinks served). Left out here: spirits are sold at prices the state sets, including a $1.25-a-proof-gallon premium; beer and hard cider pay 35 cents a gallon and wine 60 cents (sparkling wine $1.24).

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at 5.5%, on top of excise taxes left out here: $3.50 a pack of 20 cigarettes since January 5, 2026 (was $2.00), 75% of the cost price on other tobacco products, e-cigarettes and their liquids and premium cigars included (was 43%), and $3.54 an ounce on smokeless tobacco.
Diapers are taxed: bills to exempt them passed the House but died in the Senate (LD 287 in 2024; LD 1099 on April 29, 2026).
Personal care products: menstrual products (tampons, pads, panty liners, menstrual cups) have been exempt since October 1, 2021, which is not taken out here.
Barber and beauty services aren't taxed.
Clothing is taxed; Maine has no sales tax holiday.
Laundry and dry cleaning aren't taxed.
Motor fuel on which the fuel tax is paid is exempt from sales tax and pays 30 cents a gallon (gasoline) instead, left out here.
Repair labor billed separately isn't taxed; parts are.
Maine has no local sales, meals or lodging taxes; bills to let towns tax short-term lodging failed in 2024 (LD 1298) and 2025 (LD 746).
Hotel and short-term rental stays are taxed at 9%, car rentals of less than a year at 10% and adult-use cannabis at 14% (since January 1, 2026); none is counted here.
Since January 1, 2026 the former service provider tax is part of the sales tax, and streaming audio and video are taxed at 5.5%.

Maine taxes only the services its law lists (lodging, electricity delivery, vehicle extended service contracts, prepaid calling, cable and satellite TV, fabrication, telecommunications and, since January 1, 2026, streaming audio and video); haircuts, laundry and dry cleaning and car repair labor are not among them.
gaps: Maine has no local sales, meals or lodging taxes; the 5.5% general rate applies everywhere (bills to allow a local lodging tax failed in 2024 and 2025).

Prepared food, and liquor served in licensed establishments, are taxed at the state's 8% rate, counted in the restaurant categories; lodging (9%), car rentals (10%) and adult-use cannabis (14% since January 1, 2026) carry other state rates that are not part of these categories (36 M.R.S. 1811).

programs: Maine has no statewide map of its programs. Mapped: TIF districts in Auburn, Westbrook, Brunswick and South Portland (2021 layer) and Portland's downtown improvement district, from the cities' layers. Not mapped: Bangor's TIF parcels (the city's layer gives district numbers only), Ellsworth's six TIF districts (drawn only as pictures in the city's July 2026 TIF report to its council), other towns' TIF districts (the Department of Economic and Community Development's list refuses scripts) and the Maine Downtown Center's Main Street communities (no map; named on their pages). Pine Tree Development Zone benefits continue for businesses already certified (new certifications ended in 2024; benefits end December 31, 2034).

warn.text: Portland draws many visitors (the Old Port and the Casco Bay islands), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: its seasonal homes (5.9%) and its 79 lodging places (1.1 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 5 of its 20 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
